title: DSA: greedy and backtracking
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: When greedy works and how to prove it, activity selection, jump game, gas station, then subsets, permutations, combination sum with pruning and duplicate handling.
source: CLRS ch. 16; LeetCode Jump Game, Gas Station, Subsets I/II, Permutations II, Combination Sum; MIT 6.046 greedy notes; NeetCode backtracking roadmap

questions.prompt: Activities as (start, finish): (1,4), (3,5), (0,6), (5,7), (3,9), (5,9), (6,10), (8,11), (8,12), (2,14), (12,16). An activity may start exactly when another finishes. What is the maximum number of activities one person can attend?
questions.explanation: Sort by finish and pick greedily: (1,4), (5,7), (8,11), (12,16) = 4. No schedule of 5 exists; the earliest-finish rule is optimal.

questions.prompt: Gas station circuit: gas = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and cost = [3, 4, 5, 1, 2]. Station i gives gas[i] and the trip to the next station costs cost[i]. At which index (0-based) must you start to complete the circle?
questions.explanation: Total gas 15 equals total cost 15, so a solution exists. Reset the start whenever the running tank goes negative: it fails at 0, 1, 2 and the start becomes 3. From 3 the tank runs 3, 6, 4, 2, 0 and never goes negative.

questions.prompt: What does an exchange argument show about a greedy algorithm?

options.text: Any optimal solution can be reshaped into the greedy one without getting worse.
options.why: Correct: swapping in the greedy choice never reduces quality, so greedy is optimal.

options.text: The greedy choice is optimal on every random test you ran, including large ones.
options.why: Tests are evidence, not a proof; an exchange argument is a proof.

options.text: The algorithm runs in O(n log n) because it sorts the input first and then scans once.
options.why: Running time is separate from correctness; the argument is about optimality.

options.text: Every subproblem is solved once and cached in a table for later reuse.
options.why: That describes dynamic programming memoisation, not an exchange argument.

questions.explanation: For activity selection: take any optimal schedule, swap its first activity for the earliest-finishing one; it still fits and has the same size.

questions.prompt: Maximising the number of non-overlapping meetings in a room.
questions.assertion: Sort by earliest finish time, not earliest start time.
questions.reason: Finishing earliest leaves the most room for the remaining meetings, which an exchange argument proves.

whys.a: Right: R is the justification that A is the correct rule.
whys.b: R is the justification, not an unrelated fact.

questions.explanation: Earliest start fails on one long meeting that starts first and blocks many short ones.

questions.prompt: Making change with the fewest coins.
questions.assertion: Taking the largest coin that fits at each step gives the fewest coins for any coin system.
questions.reason: Largest-first is optimal for the coin system {1, 5, 10, 25}.

whys.a: A is false, so R cannot explain it.
whys.d: Right: A is false because of counterexamples like {1,5,6,9} with 11 (greedy 3 coins, optimal 2); R is true for canonical systems such as US coins.

questions.explanation: Whether greedy works depends on the coin system. For arbitrary coins use DP.

questions.prompt: True or false: to maximise the number of non-overlapping activities, always pick the shortest remaining activity first.

options.why: Correct: [1,5), [5,9) and [4,6): shortest-first takes [4,6) and gets 1, while the optimal picks [1,5) and [5,9) for 2.

questions.explanation: Only earliest-finish-time is provably optimal; earliest-start and shortest-first both have counterexamples.

questions.prompt: Write a Java method boolean canJump(int[] nums). You start at index 0 and nums[i] is the maximum jump length from index i. Return true if the last index is reachable, in O(n) time using a greedy farthest-reach variable.

checks.label: tracks the farthest reachable index with Math.max
uses i + nums[i] as the candidate reach
returns false when the current index is beyond the reach

questions.explanation: Greedy works because reachable indices form a prefix: if you can reach index r, you can reach everything before it. A backwards "goal post" loop is an equally valid O(n) solution (it would need these checks adapted). For [2,3,1,1,4] the result is true and for [3,2,1,0,4] it is false.

questions.prompt: How many distinct permutations does the multiset {A, A, B, C} have?
questions.explanation: 4! / 2! = 24 / 2 = 12. A backtracking solution that sorts the input and skips equal neighbours (using a used[] array) produces exactly 12 leaves; a naive one produces 24 with duplicates.

questions.prompt: Candidates [2, 3, 6, 7] (each may be reused any number of times) and target 7. How many distinct combinations sum to 7?
questions.explanation: [2,2,3] and [7] are the only two. Every other path either overshoots 7 or leaves a remainder of 1, which no candidate can fill. Sorting and breaking when a candidate exceeds the remainder prunes the search.

questions.prompt: Write a Java method List<List<Integer>> subsets(int[] nums) that returns all subsets (the power set) of an array of distinct integers using backtracking. You may add a private helper method.

checks.label: adds a copy of the current path to the result
chooses with add and un-chooses with remove (backtrack)

questions.explanation: The copy is essential: adding cur itself would leave every entry pointing at the same, finally empty list. There are 2^n results, each copied in O(n), so O(n * 2^n) time. An include/exclude binary recursion or a bitmask loop over 0..2^n-1 are also valid.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function combination_sum(cands, target) that returns all unique combinations of the positive integers in cands that sum to target, where each number may be reused. Sort first and prune once a candidate exceeds the remaining target.

checks.label: sorts the candidates to enable pruning
prunes with break (or return) when a candidate is too big
recurses on the same index so numbers can be reused
appends a copy of the path and pops after recursing

questions.explanation: Starting each loop at start (not 0) prevents [2,3] and [3,2] both appearing. Passing i (not i + 1) is what allows reuse. The break is valid only because the list is sorted. Immutable alternatives (cur + [x]) avoid the pop.

questions.prompt: Complete the rule for subsets of an array that may contain duplicates.
questions.text: First {1} the array. In the loop, skip nums[i] when i > start and nums[i] == nums[{2}]. A set of n distinct items has {3} subsets.
questions.explanation: Sorting groups equal values. Skipping a repeat only at the same recursion level (i > start) still allows [2,2] while removing a duplicate [2] branch. [1,2,2] yields 6 unique subsets instead of 8.

questions.prompt: Match each enumeration with the number of results (leaves) it produces.

left.text: All subsets of n distinct items
All permutations of n distinct items
All combinations of k items chosen from n
All valid strings of n pairs of parentheses

questions.explanation: Subsets: include/exclude per item. Permutations: n choices, then n-1, ... Combinations: n-choose-k. Parentheses: Catalan numbers (1, 2, 5, 14 for n = 1..4). Total work multiplies by the cost of copying each result.

questions.prompt: In Combination Sum with reusable candidates.
questions.assertion: Recursing with the same index i, not i + 1, lets a candidate be used again.
questions.reason: Each recursive call subtracts the chosen candidate from the remaining target.

whys.a: R does not explain why reuse is allowed.
whys.b: Right: both are true; reuse comes from the index, while subtracting the candidate is how the target shrinks.

questions.explanation: The index controls which candidates remain available; the remaining value controls termination. Mixing these up is a common bug.
